name: Gestrinone

lead: Gestrinone is a prescription steroid used in some countries for endometriosis and sometimes fibroids. It acts on progesterone and androgen receptors and has weak anabolic activity.

It is discussed in performance circles because of that anabolic activity and because it is the chemical precursor of the designer steroid THG. No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes.

paras: It binds the progesterone receptor strongly and the androgen receptor more weakly, suppresses the mid-cycle LH/FSH surge and ovarian steroid production, and lowers SHBG, which raises free testosterone.

Reported effects include acne, oily skin, hair loss, hirsutism, weight gain and voice deepening, some of which may be irreversible, plus menstrual suppression. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, banned in sport, and not approved in the US.

lead: Gestrinone is a synthetic steroid medication derived from 19-nortestosterone that combines progestogenic, antiprogestogenic, antiestrogenic and weak androgenic activity. It was introduced for medical use in 1986 and is marketed mainly for endometriosis, under brand names such as Dimetrose and Nemestran, in a limited number of countries; it is not available in the United States.[1][2]

Its appearance-related profile in bodybuilding and performance-enhancement circles stems from its weak anabolic and androgenic properties, which led the International Olympic Committee to ban it in sport.[1] Gestrinone is also the chemical precursor of tetrahydrogestrinone (THG), the designer steroid identified in 2003 in a doping case.[1][3]

Published clinical research concerns gynecological conditions, chiefly endometriosis, and not muscle, body composition or other appearance outcomes. Reported adverse effects are largely androgenic, including acne, oily skin, hair loss, voice deepening and menstrual suppression.[1]
infobox: Not available in the US; banned in sport

paras: Gestrinone is approved in some countries for endometriosis, where it is described as similar to danazol but with fewer androgenic side effects. It has also been used for uterine fibroids and heavy menstrual bleeding.[1] Gestrinone has also been studied as a contraceptive because it inhibits ovulation, but the largest study reported a pregnancy rate of about 4.6 per 100 woman-years, which was considered too high to recommend it for that purpose.[1]

subs.h: Use in appearance and performance contexts
paras: Gestrinone has no approved cosmetic or muscle-building indication. Its weak anabolic activity is the reason sports authorities list it as a prohibited substance.[1] No published human trials have tested it for body composition or other appearance outcomes.

A Cochrane review of progestagens and anti-progestagens for endometriosis-associated pain and reviews of endometriosis therapies discuss gestrinone among the hormonal options.[4][5] A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis summarised on Grokipedia reports that gestrinone performed comparably to danazol on pain and ovarian morphology in endometriosis.[2] Evidence concerns gynecological outcomes only.

Side effects are mainly androgenic and antiestrogenic. In one study of oral use, seborrhea (71%), acne (65%), breast hypoplasia (29%), hirsutism (9%) and scalp hair loss (9%) were reported; other effects include weight gain, voice deepening and clitoral enlargement, and voice changes, clitoral enlargement and hirsutism may be irreversible.[1] Amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea is common and estradiol levels fall by roughly half, which can cause estrogen-deficiency symptoms.[1]

Contraindications include pregnancy and lactation, severe cardiac, kidney or liver disease, and use in children.[1] The vaginal route is reported to produce fewer androgenic effects and less weight gain than oral dosing.[1]

Gestrinone binds strongly to the progesterone receptor and with lower affinity to the androgen receptor, acting as a mixed progestogen/antiprogestogen and a weak androgen. It suppresses the mid-cycle LH and FSH surge without changing basal levels, inhibits ovarian steroidogenesis, and lowers sex hormone-binding globulin, raising free testosterone.[1]
It binds to albumin, is metabolised in the liver mainly by hydroxylation into less active metabolites, and has an elimination half-life of about 27 hours.[1]

Gestrinone (also ethylnorgestrienone) is an estrane steroid, a C18 methyl derivative of norgestrienone and a C17α-ethynyl, C18-methyl derivative of trenbolone, with the formula C21H24O2.[1] Tetrahydrogestrinone (THG) was synthesised by hydrogenating gestrinone, according to the 2004 paper describing its discovery.[3] THG is described as far more potent as an androgen and progestogen than gestrinone.[1]

Gestrinone was developed in the 1970s and introduced for medical use in 1986.[1][2] It was once used extensively in Europe and is now marketed in few countries, including some in Latin America, Australia and Southeast Asia.[1]

In 2003 THG was identified in the residue of a syringe that had allegedly contained an anabolic steroid undetectable by doping tests. Researchers synthesised it from gestrinone and developed mass spectrometry methods to detect it in urine.[3][6] The FDA banned THG in 2003.[1]

The International Olympic Committee has banned gestrinone in competition because of its anabolic effects. It is not available in the United States, is pregnancy category X, and is classed as an anabolic steroid (Class C5) in Brazil.[1]

Human research on gestrinone is in gynecology. ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed phase 2 trial of a bioabsorbable subdermal gestrinone implant for endometriosis pelvic pain (n=100), a recruiting phase 4 comparison of an implant with oral dienogest for endometriosis (n=70), and a trial examining gestrinone and endothelial function in young women (n=90).[7][8][9] Earlier trials summarised in reviews examined endometriosis, fibroids and contraception.[2][4][5] No studies were found testing gestrinone for muscle growth, fat loss or other appearance goals.

timeline.event: Introduced for medical use, chiefly for endometriosis.[1]
THG, synthesised from gestrinone, identified in a doping investigation; FDA bans THG.[1][3]
Paper describes synthesis and urine detection of THG.[3]
Phase 2 trial of a gestrinone subdermal implant for endometriosis pain begins.[7]
